A few additional thoughts:

- When you have ordered outcomes, and you switch to conditional.x = FALSE, make sure that any binary covariates (eg gender) are included in the list of 'ordered' variables. Failing to do so may lead to the warning about 'trouble constructing W matrix'

- If you use conditional.x = TRUE (the default), there is a 'baseline.conditional.x.free.slopes' argument which is set to TRUE by default; the reasoning is that in the baseline model, the covariates may freely influence all the endogenous variables; in the user model, this is not necessarily the case (but the user has full control), potentially leading to poor fit, perhaps even worse compared to the baseline model; setting this option to FALSE will force these 'slopes' to be zero in the baseline model (inflating the CFI/TLI fit indices)

- You can always specify your own baseline model, and provide it to fitMeasures() to get the CFI/TLI fit indices

Yves.

On Tuesday, May 31, 2022 at 11:55:30 PM UTC+2 Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> Ed identified the reason your baseline.model is not nested in your target model (making it invalid for calculating incremental fit indices).  I think his solution (to treat all variable as endogenous) would make the baseline.model too restrictive by fixing all covariances among predictors to zero.  While the baseline.model can be restricted in any meaningful way, it sounds like you want to restrict endogenous with endogenous covariances to zero, but you should continue to allow exogenous with exogenous covariances to be free.  The remaining issue is how to restrict endogenous with exogenous covariances such that the baseline.model is nested in the target model.
>
> Because your predictors affect the common factors, they only have one estimated slope for all the indicators of that factor.  Because factor loadings can vary (i.e., congeneric measurement model), each predictor's (indirect) effect can vary across indicators of the same factor.  But a reasonably restricted baseline.model could constrain the effect of each predictor to equality across indicators of the same factor.  For example, the 2 indicators of the first factor:
>
> im01 ~ foo*pe08_1 + bar*pe08_3 + ... + baz*s3_3
> im21 ~ foo*pe08_1 + bar*pe08_3 + ... + baz*s3_3
>
> Then the same concept for indicators of each other factor.  You can verify that this baseline.model is nested in the target model using semTools::net()

That part is not automated in simsem. In simsem you can run the simulation through a range of sample size and find the sample size for a specific effect size. You cannot do that to find the effect size has 80% power at a specific sample size.

You would have to do this step by step:
1- run the "normal" simulation at your sample size, with like 500 replication for the model at A effect size
2- find the power at that effect size
3- change effect size A for effect size B, and run the simulation again
4- repeat until you find the effect size at which you have

You change the effect size from A to B depending on the results of step 2. So, f the power is lower than 80% you need to increase the effect size, and if the power is larger than 80% you need to decrease the effect size

This should take a couple of steps, but still should be doable in a few models to find the desire values

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

If two different  models are fit to two different data, then it does not make sense to compare model fit.

The question of chi2 p-value is a bit controversial. There are two extremes:

chi2 is valid test and if a model has p <.05, it is not the correct model for the data and should not be interpreted
Models tend to be approximations of reality but never perfect representations. Therefore, models should not be tested for exact fit and the chi2 test that does just that should not be used at all.

You can find a lot of fights between the proponents of these two perspectives on the SEMNET email list.  Here is my take on the issue:

https://youtu.be/L-mjMlyl2Xg?t=563

What I think that if p <.05 you should do is to do diagnostics to see if the model is misspecified in a way that makes a difference. If p >.05, you can congratulate yourself for finding a rare case of model that fits close to exactly. But you still should do diagnostics. Kline 2011, chapter 8 provides an excellent discussion on this issue.

Mikko

I have no solid explanation. I often observed that if the 'theta' matrix
is diagonal, and we use the ML estimator, then we can usually (almost)
perfectly reproduce the observed variances. This is not the case for GLS
and WLS, but ULS also often results in zero residuals on the diagonal.

However, as soon as off-diagonal elements of THETA  are set free, the
residuals on the diagonal are not (all) zero any longer.

I am sure there must be a nice mathematical explanation for this, but I
have not found it (or read it) yet.

Yves.

While creating some numerical examples for illustration, I stumbled upon a strange case:

library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-11
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.

dat_cov <-
  structure(c(1.32500270874737, 0.504176370852559, 0.213499406558664,
              -0.0632368897769514, 0.504176370852559, 1.16150418811817, 0.410940167030766,
              0.25233109019432, 0.213499406558664, 0.410940167030766, 0.999612112848533,
              0.218777130133126, -0.0632368897769514, 0.25233109019432, 0.218777130133126,
              0.889965312158214),
              dim = c(4L, 4L), dimnames = list(c("x", "m1", "m2", "y"),
                                              c("x", "m1", "m2", "y")))
# Fit a serial-mediation model
mod <-
'
m1 ~ a*x
m2 ~ b1*m1
y ~ b2*m2
indirect := a * b1 * b2
'

fit <- sem(model = mod, sample.cov = dat_cov, sample.nobs = 100, fixed.x = FALSE)
coef(fit)
#>      a     b1     b2 m1~~m1 m2~~m2   y~~y   x~~x
#>  0.381  0.354  0.219  0.960  0.846  0.834  1.312

Nothing special above. Just a serial mediation model with two mediators and no direct effect. I explored the option to fix the user-defined parameter, indirect, to a value:

# Fix the indirect effect to a small value
mod2 <-
'
m1 ~ a*x
m2 ~ b1*m1
y ~ b2*m2
indirect := a * b1 * b2
indirect == 0.006
'
fit2 <- sem(model = mod2, sample.cov = dat_cov, sample.nobs = 100, fixed.x = FALSE)
coef(fit2)
#>      a     b1     b2 m1~~m1 m2~~m2   y~~y   x~~x
#>  0.458 -0.099 -0.132  0.968  1.082  0.955  1.312
parameterEstimates(fit2)[8, ]
#>        lhs op     rhs    label   est se  z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 8 indirect := a*b1*b2 indirect 0.006 NA NA     NA       NA       NA

Nothing unusual again. The indirect effect is correctly fixed to the value (.006).
I then tried to see whether the solution is sensitive to the starting values. I set the starting values to .8 of the estimates without constraint:

fit3 <- sem(model = mod2, sample.cov = dat_cov, sample.nobs = 100, fixed.x = FALSE,
            start = coef(fit) * .8)
#> Warning in lavaan::lavaan(model = mod2, sample.cov = dat_cov, sample.nobs =
#> 100, : lavaan WARNING: estimation of the baseline model failed.
coef(fit3)
#>      a     b1     b2 m1~~m1 m2~~m2   y~~y   x~~x
#>  0.361  0.332  0.050  0.960  0.846  0.862  1.312
parameterEstimates(fit3)[8, ]
#>        lhs op     rhs    label   est se  z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 8 indirect := a*b1*b2 indirect 0.006  0 NA     NA    0.006    0.006

Again, the indirect effect is fixed to .006 as expected.  (I think the warning above can be ignored because it is about the baseline model, which is relevant only when we compute incremental fix indices such as CFI.)

However, the parameter estimates are very different.

comp <- cbind(parameterEstimates(fit2)[, 1:4],
              fit2.est = formatC(parameterEstimates(fit2)$est, digits = 3, format = "f"),
              fit3.est = formatC(parameterEstimates(fit3)$est, digits = 3, format = "f"))
comp
#>        lhs op     rhs    label fit2.est fit3.est
#> 1       m1  ~       x        a    0.458    0.361
#> 2       m2  ~      m1       b1   -0.099    0.332
#> 3        y  ~      m2       b2   -0.132    0.050
#> 4       m1 ~~      m1             0.968    0.960
#> 5       m2 ~~      m2             1.082    0.846
#> 6        y ~~       y             0.955    0.862
#> 7        x ~~       x             1.312    1.312
#> 8 indirect := a*b1*b2 indirect    0.006    0.006

Moreover, it seems that fit3 should be the preferred solution because its fmin is smaller than fit2:

fitMeasures(fit2, c("fmin", "chisq", "pvalue"))
#>   fmin  chisq pvalue
#>  0.230 45.992  0.000
fitMeasures(fit3, c("fmin", "chisq", "pvalue"))
#>   fmin  chisq pvalue
#>  0.052 10.364  0.035

Is there any information available from functions like lavInspect() that may hint us that we should try other starting values? If the data is real data, we may just stop at fit2 and report the results.

-- Shu Fai

P.S.: The phenomenon above seems to be restricted to a very small range of values to which the indirect effect is fixed to. Nevertheless, I think what matters in this case is not which value we fix the indirect effect to.

Thanks for your quick advice.

Not sure if this is useful. I sometimes use OpenMx. It has the fucntion mxTryHard() which will fit a model several times with randomly perturbed starting values. Maybe a similar function can be developed for lavaan? This is a draft one to illustrate the idea:

try_more <- function(object, attempts = 3, seed = NULL, rmin = .5, rmax = 1) {
    set.seed(seed)
    ptable <- lavaan::parameterTable(object)
    i_free <- ptable$free > 0
    i_free_p <- i_free & (ptable$op != "~~")
    k <- sum(i_free_p)
    ptable$est <- ptable$start
    x <- replicate(attempts, stats::runif(k, rmin, rmax), simplify = FALSE)
    out0 <- lapply(x, function(x) {
                      ptable_i <- ptable
                      ptable_i[i_free_p, "est"] <- ptable[i_free_p, "est"] * x
                      # Should do something to reject "bad" starting values
                      stats::update(object, start = ptable_i,
                                    check.start = FALSE)
                    })
    out0 <- c(list(object), out0)
    # Need to add some error catching code. It is possible that all of them fail the check.
    fit_ok <- sapply(out0, lavaan::lavInspect, what = "post.check")
    out1 <- out0[fit_ok]
    fit_fmin <- sapply(out1, lavaan::fitMeasures, fit.measures = "fmin")
    out2 <- out1[which(fit_fmin == min(fit_fmin))]
    # Should add more diagnostic information
    out2[[1]]
  }

This function is certainly not yet ready for use (e.g., error checking need to be added, need a more robust way to change the starting values, etc.) but is sufficient to illustrate the idea, I think.

If the model does not take a long time to fit, maybe this can be done whenever a model is fitted, to check automatically whether the results are sensitive to the starting values.

If convergence failed, maybe this can also be done automatically to see if convergence can be achieved by changing the starting values.

Or, just like OpenMx, this can be a standalone function for users who would like to do this.

-- Shu Fai

+ p + q + r + s + t + u + v + w + x + y + z
'

f1 =~e + x + a + g + c + q + y + w + d + u + s + v + z + h + b + j + o
f2 =~ f + i + p + t + r + n + l + m + k
'

# General factor
general =~ a + b + c + d + e + f + g + h + i + j + k + l + m + n + o
+ p + q + r + s + t + u + v + w + x + y + z

# Individual uncorrelated factors (as per the correlated factors model)
f1 =~e + x + a + g + c + q + y + w + d + u + s + v + z + h + b + j + o
f2 =~ f + i + p + t + r + n + l + m + k

general ~~ 0*f1
general ~~ 0*f2
f1 ~~ 0*f2
'
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Final models and reliability analyses used for the paper - using polychoric correlations

# Single dimension
f1.ord <- cfa(dim1, data = data2)
summary(f1.ord, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

# Correlated factors model - equivalent to EFA model
f2.ord <- cfa(dim2, data = data2)
summary(f2.ord, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

summary(f3.ord, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

> found bizarre stuff when examining its hierarchical omega using omegaFromSem() function. It says the omega total equals 1.33 while its hierarchical omega is 2.29. Since those values are implausible, could anyone explain why this happened?

That function is from the psych package <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/psych/index.html>, so you would have to ask its maintainer (providing data and script for a reprex).

If you install the semTools package, you could instead use the compRelSEM() function to obtain omega.
By default, it returns "hierarchical" for each factor in your model (so only pay attention to the factor of interest, or use the omit.factors= argument to suppress ones not of interest).
You can obtain omega "total" by setting return.total=TRUE, which assumes that you are creating a composite from ALL indicators in your model (unless you omit any using the omit.indicators= argument).
The way I designed the compRelSEM() function, I doubt values > 1 are possible.  Perhaps your measurement model has cross-loadings?  I think that might make values > 1 possible when using the original formula based on simple structure, which might be what the psych package assumes.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

SHV ~ PUB + SS + PUBxSS

Thanks in advance!

Aziz-Kaan Dönmez

Hi all,

I'm doing an analysis that has census tract level data on some environments, racial composition (in %), demographics, and health outcomes. I want to build a mediation model to test the environmental factors can be a mediator for race and health outcomes.

I also want to have random intercepts for states, considering the baseline of the metrics might vary from state, so I used the cluster parameter. Now I have two ways to build models.

The first kind is to build a model for each individual race. For example:

model_Black <- '
  # mediator
 prop_dilapbldg ~ a*Black + log.median.house.income + Pct_college + Age + Pct_Female + Pct_insurance + Pct_Owner + Pct_Vacant + Pct_SingleFam + Urban_Rural_New

  # full model
 mhlth_crud~ c*Black + log.median.house.income + Pct_college + Age + Pct_Female + Pct_insurance + Pct_Owner + Pct_Vacant + Pct_SingleFam + Urban_Rural_New + b*prop_dilapbldg

  # direct effect
  direct := c

  # indirect effect
  indirect := a*b

  # total effect
  total := c + (a*b)'

fit_Black <- sem(model_Black, data = df_sem_mhlth_crud, cluster = "State_fct")

The second is put all races in one model and define their direct/indirect effects all in one model.

model_All <- '
  # mediator

Hello,
I have a fairly complex mediation model (multilevel mediated moderation with categorical/nominal exogenous variables) and I want to ensure I am setting it up correctly.

At a high level, I want to know if differences in several beliefs help account for (mediate) why people of different political orientations have different moral judgments of various statements.

The actual study is setup as follows:
Participants rate a random 20/40 possible statements on: how immoral they are ('immoral'), and several other beliefs related to the statements ('disadvantage.sc <http://disadvantage.sc>' and 'freq.sc <http://freq.sc>' in this example) -- these are all continuous variables.
Each participant also reports their political orientation ('pol.c' here) - again, a continuous variable.
For this example, I cut the dataset down to only 3 out of the 40 statements to simplify.
Because statement is a categorical variable, I created two dummy variables ('s1' and 's2') to capture the statement effect, and then multiplied these by the political orientation score to create two dummy interaction variables ('polXs1' and 'polXs2')

An image of the head of the dataset is attached.

In doing some regression models, morality judgments depend on the interaction of political orientation and statement. The other beliefs ('disadvantage.sc <http://disadvantage.sc>' and 'freq.sc <http://freq.sc>') also depend on the interaction of political orientation and statement.

I want to know if these other beliefs mediate this interaction's effects on moral judgments. I don't care about differences between statements, or differences between beliefs. I just want a single test of whether considering these beliefs helps mediate these effects (e.g. so I can say that if you accounted for all these belief differences, people of different political orientations would have more similar moral judgments).

Here is my model.

lavMed <- '
level: 1
  # direct effect on moral judgements (interaction is effect of interest, main effects there to control for them)
  immoral ~ pol.c + s1 + s2 + c1*polXs1 + c2*polXs2

  # mediators - the two other beliefs (interaction is effect of interest, main effects there to control for them)
  disadvantage.sc <http://disadvantage.sc> ~ pol.c + s1 + s2 + dis_a1*polXs1 + dis_a2*polXs2
  freq.sc <http://freq.sc> ~ pol.c + s1 + s2 + freq_a1*polXs1 + freq_a2*polXs2

  #mediators predicting outcome
  immoral ~ dis_b*disadvantage.sc <http://disadvantage.sc> + freq_b*freq.sc <http://freq.sc>

  # total indirect effect (a*b) for each statement dummy code, summed over all mediators
  tot_ab1 := dis_a1*dis_b + freq_a1*freq_b
  tot_ab2 := dis_a2*dis_b + freq_a2*freq_b

  # total effect (total effect of interaction of politics and statement, for each statement dummy code)

  total2 := c2 + tot_ab2

level: 2

  immoral ~~ immoral + disadvantage.sc <http://disadvantage.sc> + freq.sc <http://freq.sc>
  disadvantage.sc <http://disadvantage.sc> ~~ disadvantage.sc <http://disadvantage.sc> + freq.sc <http://freq.sc>
  freq.sc <http://freq.sc> ~~ freq.sc <http://freq.sc>
'

           data = d_tmp,

summary(fit)

con = '
   tot_ab1 == 0
   tot_ab2 == 0
'
lavTestWald(fit, constraints = con)

Some things I am not sure about:
-Political orientation is technically a level 2 variable, though I am only including the main effect of politics to control for it. Is it fine to put it where I have it in the level 1 model and not in the level 2 model?

-Is the omnibus test on my indirect effects the correct way to test my conceptual question and get a single value for the indirect effects being significant or not?

Aside from this, is there anything else I got incorrect?

Any feedback would be much appreciated!
Thalia

messages.subject_clean: Colon operator and moderated mediation
messages.body_plain:
Another belated reply.

The use of the 'colon' operator is dangerous. It is one of those syntax
'features' that I regret. It was only intended for interaction terms
involving 1) two, 2) exogenous, 3) observed variables. It is much safer
to define the product terms in the data.frame beforehand, and avoid the
use of the colon operator altogether.

However, lavaan dev 0.6-12 will now check the status (dependent or
independent) of both variables in the interaction term, and if either
one (or both) are dependent, the interaction term is no longer treated
as exogenous (ie., it will not appear in the output of lavNames(fit,
"ov.x"))

As a result, it shouldn't be a problem to add the residual covariance
between the mediator (M) and the interaction term (M:W), even if fixed.x
= TRUE.

This term will not be added automatically, as M:W does not appear in
either lavNames(,"ov.x") or lavNames(,"ov.y").

As for the second question ("Is there an option that can force lavaan to

set all the covariances between the exogenous variables free, even if we

manually set some covariances to free?"), the answer is: "no".

If variables are correctly identified as being exogenous, there is no
need. Once you intervene manually, the user is responsible for adding
all the needed covariances. This may be error-prone, but the 'automagic'
completion of model syntax can only go so far.

Yves.
